data.title: Mouse Prefontal Cortex Astrocyte Proteome
data.projectDescription: Anxiety disorders are among the most common and disabling mental health disorders worldwide with inadequate therapeutic options. Numerous clinical and research studies indicate essential neuronal contribution to anxiety, yet the mechanisms of non-neuronal cells governing this emotional state remain poorly understood. Here, we show that non-neuronal astrocytes in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) encode anxiogenic environmental cues. Silencing mPFC astrocyte Ca2+ signaling heightens anxiety-like behavior and disrupts the balance between excitatory and inhibitory neuronal population activity. Moreover, this effect is differentially pronounced across behaviorally tuned neuronal subpopulations on single cell and network levels. Using cell type-specific proximity-dependent biotinylation approaches, we further identified significant protein expression changes in astrocytes and at the astrocyte-neuron interface within the mPFC.
data.sampleProcessingProtocol: Proximity-dependent biotinylation labeling experiments with TurboID were performed as previously described with some modifications. Three to four weeks after AAV microinjection, biotin (Sigma; B4501) was subcutaneously injected at 24 mg/kg for 3 times over 24 h. For astrocyte cytosolic protein purification, brain tissue containing the mPFC from 3 mice was pooled as one replicate. For interface protein purification, mPFC brain tissue from 4 mice was pooled as one replicate. Tissue was homogenized with 500 µl of lysis buffer-A (50 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 1mM EDTA, 1X Halt Protease Inhibitor (Thermo; 78425)), an equal volume of lysis buffer-B (50 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 0.4% SDS, 2% TritonX-100, 2% deoxycholate) was added. The homogenate was sonicated for 20 s and centrifuged at 15,000 g for 15 min at 4°C. Supernatant was further ultracentrifuged at 100,000 g for 30 min at 4°C (Beckman TLA-100 ultracentrifuge, TLA-100.3 rotor). SDS was added to the cleared supernatant to a final concentration of 1% and the samples were heated at 95°C for 5 min. Samples were then cooled down on ice and incubated with 10 µl of Pierce Streptavidin magnetic beads (Thermo Fisher; 88817) at 4°C overnight. Beads were washed twice with 2% SDS, twice with 1% TritonX-100, 1% deoxycholate, 25 mM LiCl, twice with 1M NaCl, 5 times with 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate, and 3 times with 20 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl. Magnetic beads were then centrifuged at 2,000 g for 2 min and trypsinized and subjected to LC-MS/MS analysis.The quantitative LC-MS/MS analysis was adapted from previously published work Protein digestion was carried out directly after protein purification. Dithiothreitol (DTT) was added to the beads to a final concentration of 10 mM. The samples were then incubated at 60 °C for 30 min, and iodoacetamide was added to the sample to a final concentration of 15 mM. Next, samples were incubated again for 30 min at room temperature in the dark. DTT was added to the samples to a final concentration of 20 mM. The samples were incubated with the DTT-containing buffer for 30 min at room temperature in the dark to quench the alkylation reaction. Sequencing grade modified trypsin (Promega, Madison, WI) was spiked into each sample at an enzyme/protein ratio (w/w) of 1:20. The samples were digested for 16 h in a 37 °C water bath. After the incubation, the enzymatic reaction was quenched by adding 1 μl of formic acid, leading to a pH adjustment to 3−4. The samples were dried in the vacuum concentrator (Eppendorf). Then, the dried protein digests were reconstituted in 200 μl of 0.1% formic acid in water, then the samples were desalted using Pierce peptide desalting spin columns (ThermoFisher Scientific), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The tryptic peptides were eluted from the spin columns with 600 μl of 50/50/0.1 acetonitrile/water/FA mixture. The eluate was dried completely in the vacuum concentrator.
data.dataProcessingProtocol: The acquired raw data from each LC-MS analysis were imported onto PEAKS Online (Bioinformatics Solutions Inc., Waterloo, ON) for peptide identifications. The selected protein database for Mus musculus was downloaded from UniProt. The following parameters were employed for de novo peptide sequencing and protein identification via database search: precursor mass error tolerance = 20 ppm, fragment mass error tolerance = 0.05 Da, enzyme = trypsin, digest mode = specific, peptide length was set between 6 and 45 residues, and the maximum number of missed cleavages was set to 3. Carbamidomethylation of cysteine residues was set as a fixed modification. Hexose of lysine, or arginine residues was set as a variable modification. Search result filters were set to a peptide discovery rate (FDR) of 1%, and a protein filter was set to −log10(P value) > 20. Interface proteins were filtered with a confidence score ≧ 4 for extracellular or plasma membrane localization.  For label-free quantitation, the PEAKS LFQ module was employed to extract the peak areas of the peptides in each sample. Parameters for the PEAKS Q quantitation were as follows: mass error tolerance = 20 ppm, retention time shift tolerance was set to “auto detect”, collisional cross section (CCS) error tolerance = 0.05, and feature intensity ≥ 300. The following peptide filters were selected: average area ≥ 300, peptide ID count ≥ 2, charge between 1 and 10, have at least 2 confident samples per group, and use in group coefficient of variation filter. For protein abundance calculations, the top 3 highest peptide peak areas were averaged for each unique protein. The protein peak areas obtained from PEAKS LFQ were imported onto the Normalyzer (version 1.14.0) online tool for normalization, whereby peak areas were log2 transformed and then normalized by variance stabilization normalization (VSN). This normalization method has been shown to be well-suited for label free quantitation proteomics for reducing the intragroup variation for accurate quantitation.
